title: Bezos has written his way around profit for 20 years. Has anyone else learned the trick?
excerpt: Telling one story for 20 years without changing it is a skill in itself.
body:
Telling one story for 20 years without changing it is a skill in itself.

Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos's [annual letter to shareholders is out again](http://www.forbes.com/sites/ryanmac/2016/04/05/jeff-bezos-calls-amazon-best-place-in-the-world-to-fail-in-shareholder-letter/#36e5365162f4).

This time his point is that years of bets have paid off: in 2015 Amazon passed US$100 billion in annual revenue, and its market value pulled away from Walmart's. Both came out of the fast growth of cloud computing and Prime — risks almost no one believed in at the time.

In the letter, Bezos reminds investors:

> “Nine out of ten risks may end in failure, but if there is a one-in-ten chance of a hundredfold return, you have to bet everything, every time.”

That is barely different from [the first shareholder letter he wrote, in 1997](http://media.corporate-ir.net/media_files/irol/97/97664/reports/Shareholderletter97.pdf). From then on Bezos pushed bold investment and refused to hurry toward short-term profit: “At this stage, we are putting the emphasis on growth.”

Not many people realized that “this stage” would last 20 years:

![Amazon's revenue and profit, 2005–2015. Note that the profit — or rather the absence of it — continues to this day. Set against Amazon, every “rule” about price-to-earnings ratios turns into a joke](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171915snq6HtSA3BD9uwec.jpg-w600)

There has been no profit, yet Amazon's share price has risen more than a thousandfold, which means the market accepted what Bezos said.

![Amazon's share price, 2005–2016](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171915NhLkS3VsGouv4TQ6.jpg-w600)

Not having to please the market with profit means Amazon can spend its money on the core business and on building the next ones. No other company has managed that for 20 years running.

“Amazon has used storytelling to get the cheapest capital in human history,” says Scott Galloway, a professor at New York University's Stern School of Business. Profit, he says, is like heroin: once investors are used to a company making money, they cannot stomach a story about giving up profit to take market share.

Walmart is a good example. Under pressure from e-commerce, it spent the past two years trying to copy Amazon — thinning its margins and spending the money on the fight — and its stock dropped sharply.

Twenty years of zero profit, and sometimes losses, let Amazon's core business, e-commerce, leave its rivals in Europe and the US far behind. At the same time it put the revenue into one new business after another: the Kindle, cloud computing, video.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016070217191650hvkbaQDrdoPlTx.jpg-w600)

Bezos really can tell a story. This week's letter makes the case for risk again, this time with a picture you can see:

> “In baseball, swinging for the far fence makes you more likely to miss, but it also gives you a shot at a home run. The difference between baseball and business is that one swing is worth four runs at most. In business, the payoff can be 1,000 times.”

But writing letters is not by itself enough to make investors accept zero profit, forgo dividends and wait for a return years away.

After the Fire Phone failed in 2014, the doubts kept coming and the stock fell for a full year. Then, in early 2015, Amazon broke out the numbers for its cloud business in its financial statements, showing a business that threw off billions of dollars of net profit a quarter — and the market was again convinced by Bezos's logic that you win some bets and lose some, but the wins can be very large.

An earnings report uses a handful of key numbers to show how the main businesses are doing. When those numbers match the attractive story management tells, the story becomes convincing. Better still if the story can keep going. The one in Bezos's letter has kept going for 20 years.

Amazon is not the only company trying to turn a story into more capital. The biggest tech companies in China and the US all want the market to accept their own business logic. Look at how each has fared and you can see it is not easy.

## Apple: the shift from selling devices to selling services is a story that doesn't hold together

Outside the company, Apple is seen as a device maker — one that sells more and more high-margin devices.

That used to be fine. The iPod, iPhone and iPad arrived one after another, and Apple could keep shareholders with it while paying no dividend. The iPhone above all: no other product on earth has made more than US$10 billion of profit in a single quarter.

The problem now is that the iPhone story is close to finished. It can no longer promise to sell more every quarter.

![The iPhone's year-on-year growth rate fell below 1% for the first time in the fourth quarter of 2015](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171916Plo062m54zrI8kjq.jpg-w600)

On January's earnings call, Tim Cook tried to go around the question. Instead of saying how much better the 6s sold than the 6, he said the latest quarter's sales were 1.5 times those of “two years ago.”

Why reach back two years? Because against the year before, iPhone sales were up 0.4%. That game cannot get past investors or the press.

The new story Cook has found for Apple is services.

In [a set of slides](http://images.apple.com/pr/pdf/q1fy16supplementalmaterial.pdf) released with the last quarterly results of 2015, Apple gave a whole page to one large number: 1 billion active devices.

![A page from Apple's latest quarterly earnings supplement. The 1 billion active devices include the iPhone, iPad, Mac, iPod touch, Apple TV and Apple Watch](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021719172LqlsdVJfCYIgDNU.jpg-w600)

Those 1 billion devices, [Cook said](http://seekingalpha.com/article/3836826-apples-aapl-ceo-tim-cook-q1-2016-results-earnings-call-transcript?page=3), are the base on which Apple sells services, and selling services is Apple's future.

But Cook picked the wrong moment to tell it. As the financial analyst Neil Cybart put it, Apple's management should not have waited until growth stopped to change Wall Street's mind; they could see the trend coming earlier and should have started talking about growth beyond hardware sooner.

And while Cook was explaining how much services matter, the statements Apple put out said nothing clear about which services were doing well. Advertising revenue? The change in paid subscribers? App Store revenue? Not one of them was spelled out. The only clear figures were for devices — the iPhone, the iPad.

A run of recent events points the same way: Apple News [cannot tell how many people read an article](http://www.wsj.com/articles/apple-news-app-is-off-to-a-rocky-start-1452474159), partners have [said the paid video service is going badly](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/14360.html), and iAd has been restarted again and again. The impression is of a company better at hardware than at services.

Nobody is going to shake Apple's enviable hardware business any time soon. But if people are to treat it as a services company, Cook's story is not good enough yet.

## Alibaba: in the end, the talk came back to e-commerce

Alibaba went public in the summer of 2014, and for most of the year that followed its share price fell.

The reason for the gloom was simple: Alibaba was taken for one big e-commerce company, and inside it there were mainly two businesses, Taobao and Tmall.

Both were thought to have problems. The fight over counterfeits on Taobao never stopped. Tmall, which carries the higher margin, kept growing more slowly than JD.com:

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171917El0jzADUrv7B36oY.jpg-w600)

Add worries about a slowing Chinese economy, and slowing consumption with it, and Alibaba's share price is still below its offer price today.

In October 2015 Alibaba started trying to change the market's mind. Timed to the first anniversary of the listing, Jack Ma wrote [an open letter of more than 4,000 characters](http://ar.alibabagroup.com/2015/letter-cn.html) telling this story: Alibaba is not only an e-commerce company.

> “Today the Cainiao logistics system Alibaba has invested in already helps handle some 10 billion parcels a year; our internet finance business serves nearly 400 million active users; our cloud computing business is among the world's leaders and is still growing more than 100% a year; and our mobile internet basics — search, maps, browsers — provide services Chinese users cannot do without.”

> What we are building is the infrastructure of future commerce. We empower the merchants who buy and sell rather than compete with them, and in that sense the so-called “competitors” in today's market are the very ones we will empower and help in future. To put it another way, treating today's e-commerce companies as Alibaba's rivals is like comparing an apple with an apple tree, which does justice to neither.

The apple tree is a fine image. The only trouble is that the apples on it — the finance business Ant Group, valued at US$50 billion, and Cainiao, reportedly worth 50 billion yuan — were both carved out before Alibaba listed. Alibaba holds only part of Ant Group and part of Cainiao Network.

Which is to say they are other companies' businesses. They can make Jack Ma richer, but they will not bring Alibaba's shareholders much directly.

By 2016 the story had swung back to e-commerce — to e-commerce sales figures of better quality.

Last month Alibaba announced that transaction volume for its 2016 fiscal year had passed 3 trillion yuan. Vice chairman Joe Tsai said: “We have therefore shifted our focus to quality growth and to broadening domestic consumption. That means the way we measure success no longer rests on a simple view of GMV growth.”

## Alphabet: accepting Wall Street's rules

Google has always been read as an advertising company — more precisely, a PC advertising company.

That was fine in itself. On the steady income of search advertising, Google could spend heavily on long-term projects full of imagination, even when those projects earned nothing.

So we got the futuristic new businesses: Google Glass, the smart-home company Nest, artificial intelligence, life sciences, driverless cars, and on and on.

Wall Street did complain, often, that Google was opaque and would not disclose what the new businesses earned. But year after year the advertising revenue came in higher, and the share price went up with it.

The smartphone and the rise of Facebook changed how Google was seen.

As the internet moved from the computer to the phone, search mattered less, and social networks were taken to be the future home of mobile advertising. In the global digital advertising market, Google's share and Facebook's have been moving in opposite directions:

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171918LyxHhlJ7gGQqjWK6.jpg-w600)

This is the first time since Google got into advertising that another company has taken share from it. Look only at the US market, and only at mobile advertising, and Facebook's impact is larger still.

Remember, too, that Facebook so far makes money only from its own network. It has not begun to work the advertising potential of Instagram and WhatsApp, each with hundreds of millions of users:

![Where Facebook's revenue came from, 2015. Chart by [L2](https://www.l2inc.com/speakers/scott-galloway)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171918eByM2XlszPvDHmwY.jpg-w600)

From 2015 the pressure began to change Google. First it replaced its CFO and started cutting day-to-day costs. Then, overnight, it announced a reorganization into Alphabet.

After the reorganization, the core businesses that make money from advertising — Google search, Chrome, Android, YouTube — stayed inside Google. The other small companies, their futures unclear and their bills paid by advertising, were set loose to sink or swim on their own numbers.

Google's finances are now reported separately from those of the other subsidiaries, and for the first time investors can see where the money Google earns actually goes.

And if those future businesses use Google's resources, [they have to pay for them](http://www.wsj.com/articles/google-parent-to-ask-subsidiaries-to-pay-for-corporate-services-1448325619).

Google, or Alphabet, has accepted Wall Street's rules.

## Baidu: the attempt to threaten Wall Street failed

Baidu's old glory and its present trouble both look like Google's.

There was a time when Baidu decided which sites Chinese internet users visited and which services they used, and its desktop advertising carried a confidence that needed no explaining.

Then came the same move from the computer to the smartphone, and Baidu was suddenly behind. Its place as the internet's main gateway was taken by WeChat.

![Tencent's advertising business has grown more than 100% year on year for the past three quarters](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702171919KDbWuESUoyPxf1hM.jpg-w600)

With WeChat and Qzone behind it, Tencent's advertising has closed the gap fast. In each of the past three quarters its online ad revenue has doubled from a year earlier.

Unlike Google, Baidu was late to every turn in the market after search — mobile, app stores, local services.

Robin Li has tried to build new businesses — iQiyi video, Baidu Waimai food delivery, Nuomi group buying, Trip.com Group travel — all of them attempts at revenue beyond search advertising.

The problem is plain: every one of them burns cash, and nothing guarantees Baidu will win any of those fights. The result is that over the past two years Baidu's advertising revenue has grown while its profit has thinned, and the share price has fallen with it.

Interviewed by Bloomberg last September, [Robin Li said](http://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-09-13/baidu-s-li-says-investors-don-t-get-china-s-coming-internet-boom) that American investors do not understand O2O, and that he would consider delisting and going back to China: “If one day I find the US market has entirely lost any hope of sharing our values, and the domestic market truly understands our business, I might do it. But first we should be patient and give US investors some time. I hope they will come to understand us better.”

Over the two months that followed, investors did not change their minds because of the delisting threat. The stock kept falling.

In the end it was Baidu that gave ground. Late last year Qunar, which Baidu had invested in, ended its fight with Trip.com Group through a share swap. Early this year the video site iQiyi was taken private and delisted. Two cash-burning businesses out of Baidu's accounts, no longer weighing on its results.

The day after the iQiyi privatization was announced, Baidu's shares rose more than 8%. Baidu Waimai, which took market share on heavy subsidies from Baidu, has recently been reported to be raising money on its own.

But shedding the businesses that burn cash only buys one good set of results. Unless Baidu finds a way to stop the growth of Tencent's advertising, or finds a new business with a future, it ends up as another Yahoo.

## Facebook and Tencent: the challengers don't have to worry about storytelling yet

Apple, Alphabet, Amazon and Facebook in the US; Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent in China — these are taken to be the most important tech giants in each country.

For now, only Tencent and Facebook have spent little effort talking to investors.

In the move from the computer to the phone, social networks shook the once-solid positions of Google and Baidu, and Facebook and Tencent were the ones who gained from the shift.

Nor are they like Amazon, pushing to put every bit of revenue back into the fight.

Both still have a lot of room to grow. Until that runs out, they do not need to worry about how to tell a story. The numbers in the financial statements are convincing enough.

A monopoly on a market with a future is always the best story.

Charts by Zhao Changcun / cover image from [CNBC](http://www.cnbc.com/2015/01/12/happy-birthday-jeff-bezos-heres-another-15-million.html)
